confidence_why: Hualde's accent chapter in the 2003 Mouton reference grammar, his 1997 monograph on Basque accentuation, the 2015 acoustic study by Gandarias, Gaminde, Unamuno and Iglesias of a Standard-Basque speaker and Munarriz's 2006 study of an Ataun speaker all put the default accent on the second syllable of the word in Standard and central Basque, while the lexical pitch accent systems of Northern Bizkaian (Elordieta and Selkirk 2018, Ito 2002, Wolf 2008) and the penultimate accent of the eastern dialects (Hualde 1997) are other dialects, not disagreements about this record. Souletin is described separately below, with a different pattern. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Hualde 2003 2003.

catalog_quote: [p. 71] In a large central area covering most of Gipuzkoa and parts of Bizkaia and Navarre, the general rule is postinitial accent (on the second syllable), with some exceptional words receiving, instead, initial accent. The general pattern is illustrated by examples such as gizóna 'the man', gizónari 'to the man', gizónarena 'the one of the man', txistúlaria 'the flutist', txistúlariari 'to the flutist'. In most varieties with postinitial accent, final prominence is avoided, with accent retraction to the initial syllable in bisyllabic forms: néska 'the girl', neskári 'to the girl'. ... In Standard Basque, postinitial accent is the dominant pattern among speakers of this variety. [p. 102] Stress is generally post-initial, i.e., on the second syllable of the word, although some exceptional words show initial stress. When the second syllable is word-final, however, stress is retracted to the first syllable ... For example: men.dí.a 'the mountain', bu.rú.a.na 'of the head', u.dá.re.a 'pear', gi.zó.na.na 'of the man', but mén.di 'mountain', bú.ru 'head', gí.zon 'man'. [p. 65] In Standard Basque, stress or accent is not phonologically contrastive. Usually the stress falls on the second syllable of the word or phrase, frequently with secondary prominence on the last syllable ... Bisyllabic words ending in a vowel receive initial stress instead; e.g. néska 'girl'. But, as mentioned, stress is not phonologically contrastive and may also fall on other syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: For Gipuzkoan Basque (the dialect of all his examples, fn. 2 p. 61) de Rijk declines to give a stress rule: the system of stress assignment is unknown, varies village to village, and stressed syllables have very little acoustic prominence; he quotes Michelena (Fonética Histórica Vasca ch. 20, p. 379) that in the central and western dialects intensity/pitch/duration differences are small and the distinctive value of the accent is reduced. The one regularity he asserts: relativized finite verb forms (zutén liburua, zetorrén gizona, dutén, datorrén) take final stress as a rule, not because of the underlying -n+n cluster; non-relativized forms sometimes also get final stress, so intonation is not a foolproof marker of relativization. Fn. 4 (p. 62) speculates that final stress was originally limited to past-tense relativized forms and spread to present-tense forms by analogy. 'Guipúzcoan' normalises the scanned garble 'Guiptzcoan'; 'ocasionally' is as printed/scanned.
new_statements.exceptions: relativized verb forms occasionally lack the expected final stress; non-relativized verb forms frequently also take final stress; strong village-to-village variation; low acoustic prominence of stress generally

new_statements.quote: Hualde (1996) argues for an example in the Basque dialect of Ondarroa. [...] Phrasal accents normally are assigned to the penultimate syllable of the phrase. However, when the underlying phrase-final vowel has been deleted in hiatus, the final vowel of the phrase has the phrasal accent: (46) /gure abare-a/ ⟶ [gure abarí] 'our priest' [...] Word-level accent behaves differently, though. There is a distinction between accented and unaccented roots in Ondarroa Basque, and the accents of accented roots normally fall on the penult syllable of the word, with affixal vowels like the determiner /-a/ counting to define which is the penult: (47) /'indarr-a/ ⟶ [inddárra] 'the bean' [...] However, when the word-final vowel is deleted in hiatus, it's the surface penult (underlying antepenult) vowel of accented words that gets the word accent: (48) /'eskola-a/ ⟶ [eskóli] 'the school'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Secondary report (after Hualde 1996, Lingua 99) of the Ondarroa (western Bizkaian) dialect: roots are lexically accented or unaccented; an accented word bears its accent on the penultimate syllable of the word (suffix vowels such as the determiner -a count), computed after hiatus-driven vowel deletion; otherwise prominence is phrasal, on the penultimate syllable of the phrase, computed before that deletion. new_statements.rule_in_words: Literature-based rule for Standard Basque (Batua), after Aurrekoetxea et al. 2015 and Hualde & Elordieta 2014: no lexically contrastive accent; stress on the second syllable from the left by default; in bi- and trisyllables a heavy final syllable (diphthong or closed: limói, balkói, esán) takes the stress, otherwise the final syllable is extrametrical, so light disyllables are initial-stressed (érre) and etxéa, ikúsi are second-syllable; whole words (not roots) are the accentual unit; downstep at phrase level. The thesis's own production data (6 Bilbao-area Basque-Spanish bilinguals, words in isolation) only partly bear this out: light-light disyllables vary freely between initial and second-syllable stress within and across speakers, LH disyllables are uniformly final(=second)-stressed, three speakers (1, 5, 6) put the F0 peak on the first syllable of trisyllables (líburu, kókapen) while all lengthen the second syllable, and suffixed forms fall back to the expected second syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none described; phrase-level downstep of successive word peaks only
new_statements.exceptions: heavy final syllables attract stress in 2-3 syllable words; light-light disyllables show free intra-speaker variation (ne.ké ~ bí.de); speakers in contact with Northern Bizkaian (Ondarroa) varieties shift prominence (speaker 7 word-final in bare forms, speaker 4 third syllable); inter-speaker variation in whether suffixes count in the accentual unit; 'lexical stress' listed as a third factor (loanwords) without a word list

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ondarroa (Northern Bizkaian) Basque, after Hualde 1996: roots are lexically accented or unaccented. Lexically accented words carry a word accent on the penultimate syllable of the word (suffixes such as determiner -a count: /'indarr-a/ -> inddárra). Unaccented words receive only the phrasal accent, which falls on the penultimate syllable of the phrase (gure abarí < /gure abare-a/ after hiatus deletion). Wolf uses the data only to argue about rule ordering (phrase accent assigned before hiatus-vowel deletion, word accent after it); it is a secondary theoretical reanalysis, not a new description.
new_statements.exceptions: Interaction with Ondarroa hiatus resolution (deletion of the second vowel): when the phrase-final vowel is deleted the phrasal accent surfaces on the final syllable (gure abarí); in accented words the word accent falls on the surface penult = underlying antepenult (/'eskola-a/ -> eskóli). Unaccented roots have no word-level accent. Elsewhere (p. 3, p. 415) Ondarroa Basque is cited only for segmental processes (Côté 1999, 2000) and 'Basque word-final vowel raising' (Hualde 1989) — nothing further on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Wolf 2008's Basque accent data are exclusively the Ondarroa dialect (Northern Bizkaian, western pitch accent area), taken from Hualde 1996; the catalog's existing statement is about the eastern type (Zuberoan, Roncalese, Baztan, Ultzama). Basque prosody is dialect-specific, so the 'pitch accent' reading here applies to Ondarroa/Northern Bizkaian, not to Basque as a whole.

sources.quote: Hualde (1996) argues for an example in the Basque dialect of Ondarroa. [...] Phrasal accents normally are assigned to the penultimate syllable of the phrase. However, when the underlying phrase-final vowel has been deleted in hiatus, the final vowel of the phrase has the phrasal accent: (46) /gure abare-a/ ⟶ [gure abarí] 'our priest' [...] Word-level accent behaves differently, though. sources.quote: In some prosodic systems the o- receives the stress if the inflected verb has two syllables (26a), but it is -te which receives it if the inflected verb has only one syllable (26b). Hence, Basque discourse particles do not have inherent stress. Moreover, it is the combination of particle and inflected verb which receives stress and, therefore, they form a prosodic word. [fn 18:] The high degree of fragmentation of the Basque language also affects its prosodic pattern; this results into a system where some varieties have a [+2] system, whereas others [-2] and so on (Hualde 1997).

sources.quote: The most widespread accentual system in central and western Basque dialects is rather different from what we have just described for NBB, however. In the most common system, there is no contrast between lexically accented and unaccented words. Instead, the accent generally falls on the second or postinitial syllable, except that there may be an exceptional class of items with initial accent. That is, the accent always falls on one of the first two syllables, most commonly on the second. [...] In the Northern Bizkaian Basque (NBB) area we find a prosodic system which in many important respects resembles that of Tokyo Japanese [...] phrases are demarcated by an initial rising configuration (%L H-), with the H- tone loosely associated with the second syllable of the phrase, and accented syllables bearing a falling contour H*L [...] there is a lexical contrast between accented and unaccented words [...] in NBB phrases containing only unaccented words receive an accent on their final syllable in focus position and in isolation

sources.citation: Hualde, José Ignacio, Rajka Smiljanić & Jennifer S. Cole. 2000. On the accented/unaccented distinction in Western Basque and the typology of accentual systems. Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society 26(1) (Proceedings of BLS 26: General Session and Parasession on Aspect): 133-144. doi:10.3765/bls.v26i1.1145
sources.quote: A first feature that NB Basque dialects have in common with Tokyo Japanese is a lexical distinction between accented and unaccented words with most words belonging to the unaccented class (Hualde 1991, 1999). In addition, in both languages lexically accented words always surface with a H*+L pitch-accent on a given syllable (in NB Basque, lexically unnaccented words do not bear any pitch-accent, unless they are in final place in the preverbal focus position, on in isolation, in which case they are also associated with a H*+L contour). [...] In Basque, lexically unaccented words do not bear any pitch-accent unless they are in phrase-final preverbal position (which is the focus position), in which case they are also associated with a H*+L contour. This accent falls on the final syllable of the word in Bermeo and on the penultimate in Markina (see Hualde 2000). [...] On the basis of these data, we conclude that duration does not appear to play a role to convey accentedness in the Northern Bizkaian Basque prosodic system.

sources.quote: In Lekeitio Basque, as in Japanese, words can be accented or unaccented. [...] Accented words have penultimate stress, triggered by accented morphemes, i.e., morphemes which are specified in the lexicon as assigners of prosodic prominence on the penultimate syllable of the word they are part of. These accented morphemes can be lexical roots or suffixes. Most lexical roots in the language are unaccented, accented roots being circumscribed to borrowings from Latin or Spanish and a few native roots. (p. 515) [...] when a word contains an accented morpheme, be it a root or a suffix, the penultimate syllable is always assigned a pitch accent. (p. 516) [...] unaccented words do not carry prosodic prominence unless they are located in phrase-final position; more precisely, if they are the last word in a phrase which immediately precedes the verb. [...] Phrasal accent is realized on the last syllable of the word. (p. 518) [...] accentual prominence in Lekeitio is realized by tonal means, that is, by assigning a H*+L pitch accent to the accented syllable. sources.citation: Hualde, José Ignacio. 1991. Manuel de Larramendi y el acento vasco. Anuario del Seminario de Filología Vasca "Julio de Urquijo" 25(3): 737-749. doi:10.1387/asju.8247
sources.quote: En un gran número de localidades de habla guipuzcoana el acento no es fonológicamente contrastivo en la actualidad. Suele recaer normalmente sobre la segunda sílaba, con un acento secundario sobre la última (tanto en el singular como en el plural). A veces el acento recae sobre la primera sílaba y la última, sin que esto sea contrastivo. [...] En una amplia zona de Vizcaya, en entonación enunciativa, la frase o palabra aislada recibe un tono alto que se extiende generalmente desde la segunda sílaba hasta la sílaba que marcamos con un acento gráfico y, a partir de aquí hay una brusca caída en el tono. [...] la característica fundamental de este tipo de acentuación es que se basa en una distinción léxica entre morfemas marcados o acentuados, por una parte, y morfemas inacentuados, por la otra. [...] En palabras que solo contienen morfemas inacentuados hay generalmente prominencia en la última sílaba; pero esto es solo un efecto a nivel de frase.
sources.note: Reviews Larramendi's 18th-century description of the Western Basque accentual system and finds it largely accurate.

sources.quote: The varieties studied range from pitch-accent systems of various types, where differences in pitch patterns play an important role in the distinction between both morphological categories and lexical items, to stress-accent systems, to varieties where the prosodic facts are completely bereft of phonological relevance. [abstract, p. 275] ... El euskera de Gernika posee un sistema de acento tonal. Este sistema tiene una funcion preponderante en la distincion entre formas singulares y plurales.
